statement: Set daily carbohydrate for ultra training at about 60% of energy intake, 5-8 g/kg/day, scaled within the range to training load; periodise rather than hold the same intake every day.
appliesTo: All ultra training athletes; build and peak weeks use upper half, recovery weeks lower half (the split is an engine default)

statement: Set protein at about 1.6 g/kg/day, raised up to 2.5 g/kg/day only in the most demanding training blocks.
Default race-day fuelling floor for ultras is 150-400 kcal/h with 30-50 g/h carbohydrate and 5-10 g/h protein from varied, palatable foods, including savoury options in longer races.
appliesTo: All single-stage ultra race plans, especially 50 km to 100+ miles, as the starting plan before any gut-training tiers

statement: Offer carbohydrate above the floor in tiers: up to about 60 g/h (single source acceptable) and up to about 90 g/h only as multiple transportable carbohydrates, each tier unlocked only after it was tolerated in long training runs. Reduce the target when absolute pace or intensity is low; do not scale by body mass.
appliesTo: Athletes who choose a higher-CHO plan and have tolerated the previous tier in training; evidence is physiological and from non-ultra trials

statement: Treat 90-120 g/h as an advanced athlete opt-in flagged low-certainty: require tolerance of 90 g/h in at least a gut-training block with symptoms logged, never a default, with automatic fall-back to the last tolerated rate if symptoms rise. Do not promise a performance benefit.
appliesTo: Gut-trained athletes only; evidence from a 26-athlete trail marathon RCT, a 16-cyclist crossover and a 37-athlete trial showing no extra performance gain

statement: Offer gut training as an optional 2-4 week block ending before the key race: near-daily to several-times-weekly sessions of at least 1 h at steady (about 60% VO2max-equivalent) effort at the intended race CHO rate. The 14-day protocol with a 1 h daily session at 90 g/h reduced GI symptoms and malabsorption; session count and the step size for increasing CHO (conservative default +10 g/h, grade D) are not established.
appliesTo: Athletes planning above-floor CHO or reporting GI symptoms; not for athletes with known GI disease

statement: Describe gut training as improving tolerance and possibly performance, never as guaranteed performance gain or gut-barrier protection; intestinal injury and permeability markers did not change in the systematic review.
appliesTo: All plan copy and UI text about gut training

statement: Log GI symptoms after long runs on the 0-4 scale (none to very severe); stop increasing CHO if symptoms worsen and drop back to the last tolerated rate. A numeric stopping threshold is not evidence-based; default to stopping progression when any symptom is moderate (2) or worse for two sessions in a row.

When forecast heat is high, lower pace expectations and GI-tolerance assumptions for long runs and races, include a nausea contingency (switch to simpler fuel, slow down) and do not escalate CHO targets that day. Count sessions of at least 2 h at about 60% VO2max-equivalent as the point where GI strain and fuelling practice matter.
value: no CHO escalation in heat; nausea contingency; 2 h threshold
appliesTo: Long runs and races in hot conditions; GI symptoms were reported by 96% of 161-km runners and peaked in the hottest segment

statement: Present fluid as a reference range of 450-750 mL/h scaled up in heat, always with a 'drink to thirst, do not force fluids' rule; never generate fixed intake volumes beyond thirst. The ACSM 2% weight-loss limit is not applied in ultras.
appliesTo: All ultra race and long-run plans; sweat rate varies widely so numbers are references, not prescriptions

statement: Show sodium as a range above about 575 mg/L of fluid, labelled as taste/cramp/comfort support; do not claim it prevents hyponatremia, and never suggest sodium to offset overdrinking.
appliesTo: All ultra race plans that display electrolyte guidance; the number rests on an expert position stand, while observational data show sodium intake does not prevent EAH

statement: If weights are used, treat weight gain over pre-race as an overhydration red flag; do not treat weight loss up to about 3% of body mass as a problem and do not target zero weight change.
appliesTo: Races with weigh-ins or athletes who self-weigh; evidence from 161-km races in northern California

statement: Attach an EAH safety card to ultra plans (nausea, headache, confusion, swelling, weight gain mean seek medical care; do not drink more) and an alert for races longer than about 17 h or in heat. The engine states symptoms and directs to medical care but does not prescribe treatment.
appliesTo: All ultra plans; stronger prompt for hot races and events over 17 h where thirst-guided drinking is stated to prevent EAH only in temperate climates under 17 h

statement: Do not prescribe high-CHO or gut-training strategies to athletes with known GI disease (show a medical disclaimer), and do not apply sex-based CHO multipliers to ultra paces because the evidence is modelling at elite marathon pace.
value: no high-CHO prescription with GI disease; no sex multiplier
appliesTo: Athletes who report GI disease; all athletes for sex-based CHO scaling
